mappings.note: Student runs the blue/red litmus test on a list of samples and records the colour in a table, which is conducting an investigation and recording observations. Not LO-2, because the table is the record of the experiment, not a differentiation the student is asked to argue.
Same recording task with turmeric paper; the assessed act is performing the test and tabulating results. Not LO-9, which is about labelled diagrams and flow charts, not an observation table.

Asks the student to predict and explain why the colour changes when lemon juice goes back into a solution that lime water had turned blue, i.e. explain the neutralisation process. Not LO-7, since no word equation is required.

The discriminating work is spotting that vinegar alone among lime water, baking soda and salt solution is acidic, i.e. differentiating substances by their acid-base property. Not LO-6, because the neutralisation is assumed rather than explained.

Three unknowns must be sorted as acidic, basic or neutral from three indicator results; that is differentiating materials on the basis of their properties. Not LO-4, since the indicators are given as data and nothing is investigated.

Reads three red-rose-strip figures and labels each solution acidic, basic or neutral. Same differentiation skill as the other unknown-identification items in this batch, which the frame houses only in LO-2.

Given a three-indicator result table, name the nature of the liquid and justify it; the justification is still a property-based differentiation. Not LO-5, because no cause is sought, only the class of the substance.

A blindfolded tester must choose an olfactory indicator: the student is planning how to run the test, which is the investigation outcome. Not LO-2, since no substance is being classified here, only a method chosen.

Open task to invent invisible-ink and spray combinations and tabulate them, which is creativity in designing with available household resources. Not LO-4, because the student designs the scheme rather than carrying out a prescribed test.

Predicting that baking soda turns the red grape-juice mixture green requires explaining the neutralisation behind the colour shift. Not LO-2, because the nature of both substances is given and only the process has to be explained.

Choosing the indicator that will reveal an orange-juice message is selecting the right test for a query. Not LO-15, unlike the invisible-ink table item, because here the setup is fixed and only the revealing method is chosen.
How to prepare a natural indicator from a plant part, with an example, is verbatim the flower-extract indicator investigation named in LO-4.

Whether turmeric paper alone can separate vinegar, baking soda and sugar solution is a question about the reach of an indicator, i.e. planning an adequate investigation. Not LO-2, because the point is the test, not the three substances.
Two parts: name the nature of X from the red rose result (LO-2), then say what excess amla juice does (LO-6, neutralisation explained). Both are genuinely assessed, so both are cited.
Completes the missing cells of a flowchart, the flow-chart half of LO-9. Not LO-2, because the classification is scaffolded by the chart and the assessed act is finishing the chart.

Names the class of substance defined by turning blue litmus red, i.e. classifying materials by a property. Not LO-2, which would require contrasting two named substances rather than naming a category.
Litmus comes from lichens: knowledge of where a natural indicator is sourced, which belongs with the indicator investigation. Not LO-1, since no organism is being identified from observable features.
No change with either litmus places the substance in the neutral class; a classification item. Not LO-2, because there is no second substance to differentiate it from.
Picks the one acidic item out of three basic household solutions, which is differentiating on a property. Not LO-3, because the student is separating a list rather than naming a class.
Why litmus counts as an acid-base indicator, i.e. what makes a substance usable as an indicator. That is the query LO-4 is framed around.
Explicitly asks how bases differ from acids on litmus, the plainest differentiate-on-properties item in the batch.
The procedure for preparing lime water from chuna, settling and filtering, is laboratory preparation within the investigation. Not LO-13, because nothing is applied to daily life; it is a bench step.
Finds the non-basic member of a list of household solutions. Shares LO-2 with the other odd-one-out item because the frame offers exactly one outcome for property-based sorting of substances.
Names the class, neutral, for tap water and sugar solution. Grouped with the other class-naming recall item; the frame has only LO-3 for naming a category.

The taught point is that lichens grow only where the air is clean, i.e. they signal pollution, which is environmental sensitivity. Not LO-14, which requires the student to take a protective action rather than recognise a pollution-sensitive organism.
Sour taste as the giveaway of an acid is identifying a material by an observable feature. Not LO-2, because only one class is characterised, with no contrast drawn.

Naming citric acid as the acid in oranges and lemons is identifying what an everyday material contains. Left at competency level because LO-1 lists only appearance, texture and function features, and the acid in a fruit is not one of them.
Same kind of item for amla and its ascorbic and citric acids, and the same reason for stopping at the competency: this frame has no outcome for naming the acid inside a foodstuff.
The soapy, slippery feel of a base is identification by texture, an observable feature named in LO-1. Not LO-3, since no classification scheme is produced.

Bitter gourd is bitter yet not basic because it lacks the other properties of a base, so the student must know which properties actually define the class. Touches the testability theme of CG-SCI1, but the assessed knowledge is the property set, which is LO-2.

Testing a household floor cleaner safely with an indicator instead of tasting it is the concept applied in day-to-day life. Not LO-4, because no investigation is designed or performed; the everyday judgement is the answer.
Defines acid-base indicator for substances such as red rose extract and turmeric, the core vocabulary of the LO-4 investigation.
The crush-soak-filter preparation of red rose extract is exactly the coloured-flower-extract indicator investigation named in LO-4.
Recall of the red rose extract result in acid. It is the observation produced by the LO-4 investigation, so it stays there rather than at LO-2, where no second substance is contrasted.
Recall of the red rose extract result in base, the companion observation to the acid case; same outcome for the same reason.
Turmeric as the kitchen spice that can be turned into indicator paper: preparing an indicator from available material, the LO-4 investigation.
Turmeric paper turning red with soap solution is the recorded result of the turmeric test.
Turmeric staying yellow in acid, which is what limits turmeric to detecting bases; still the result of the same indicator investigation.

Designing a greeting card whose message appears in colour means choosing the material that will do the job, i.e. creativity in planning with available resources. Not LO-13, because the situation is a craft design, not an everyday acidity problem.
Olfactory indicators as a category of indicator; a test-method item and so LO-4 rather than LO-1, since smell here belongs to the indicator, not to the substance being identified.
